1. Jujutsu Kaisen Season 1, episodes 1–24. 2. Jujutsu Kaisen 0, the feature film. 3. Season 2, episodes 25–47. 4. Season 3, episodes 48–59 (Season 3's first part, as indexed by the official site through its March 2026 finale). The exact numbering convention may differ on a streaming service, so look for the season label and episode title.

This release order gives newcomers the original introduction to Yuji and the central curse-fighting team before shifting attention to Yuta in the film. It then returns to familiar characters in Season 2 and reaches the Culling Game in Season 3. You could watch the prequel chronologically first, but release order preserves how the franchise introduces its lore and characters.
Why JJK 0 is set earlier but works after Season 1

Jujutsu Kaisen 0 follows Yuta Okkotsu and his first year at Tokyo Jujutsu High, before Yuji's story. That makes the movie a prequel in the in-universe timeline. It is also a complete film with its own emotional center, not a collection of missing episodes that you must insert into Season 1.

After Season 1, you already understand the basic idea of cursed energy, sorcerer training and the school setting. The film then adds another perspective and shows the organization from a different angle. Watching it before Season 1 is possible, but a new viewer may have less context for the terminology and may experience certain connections differently.
At a glance: chronology versus viewing order
IN-UNIVERSE CHRONOLOGY → JJK 0 → Season 1 → Season 2 → Season 3.
RECOMMENDED FIRST WATCH → Season 1 → JJK 0 → Season 2 → Season 3.

WHY THEY DIFFER → JJK 0 is a prequel, but the television story introduces the franchise's concepts first and the movie later broadens the cast. For most newcomers, release order is the more welcoming route.
Season 2 contains two major story sections

Season 2 opens with a past-era story centered on Satoru Gojo and Suguru Geto, then returns to the present for the Shibuya Incident. This split is intentional. Do not mistake the earlier timeline for a recap film or assume the season begins with a separate spinoff; both sections are part of the main television order.

If you are watching in a service that divides Season 2 into separate parts or uses a special listing, preserve episode order within the season. The official episode index is the reference point for numbered episodes and titles. Avoid jumping directly to Shibuya because the earlier part provides character history that changes how later scenes read.
What Season 3 covers as of November 2026

Season 3 adapts the Culling Game story. The official Japanese broadcast page says it began January 8, 2026, and the official March notice identifies episode 59 as Season 3 episode 12 and its first-part finale. The official episode index lists Season 3 and the film in the same franchise navigation, which is useful when a platform catalog separates movies from TV seasons.

That is a factual status check as of November 20, 2026, not a promise about the next season's timing. A future continuation date, episode count, English dub schedule or US simulcast time should be added only after an official production or distributor notice. The series's latest available installment can vary between Japanese broadcast, US streaming and dub schedules.
Do I need recap films or theatrical compilations?

Jujutsu Kaisen has had theatrical or compilation presentations around the franchise, including a recap of earlier events paired with new material in some markets. These listings can look like required new chapters even when their core content repeats the TV series. Read the official synopsis and release note: if the film is a recap, Season 1 and Season 2 remain the correct core path.

JJK 0 is different from a recap because it tells a full prequel story centered on Yuta. It is the one movie this order intentionally includes. If a distributor announces a new original film or a compilation with a significant new scene, describe it by its official label and explain whether its story is already covered in the episodic order.
A spoiler-light path for a returning fan

If you have seen Season 1 but skipped the film, watch JJK 0 before Season 2. If you finished Season 2, continue with Season 3 from its first episode; there is no need to replay the prequel unless you want a refresher. The central order remains straightforward even if your platform uses a different season grouping.

If you have only seen the film, the best next step is Season 1 episode 1, not Season 2. The movie introduces Yuta and key concepts but it does not retell Yuji's introduction, his relationships or the main TV plot. The shared world is not a substitute for the separate lead-character storyline.

The chronology is a useful answer to a story question, but it is not a rule for a first-time audience. Release order presents the setting in the same progression the original television audience encountered, then uses the film to deepen the world before Season 2 expands the conflict. If you have already watched the series out of order, there is no need to restart; simply watch the film before moving on to Season 2.
Where to stream in the US

US rights, subscription catalogs and dubs can change. Search the full title “Jujutsu Kaisen 0” separately from the Season 1 and Season 2 page; a service may not package the movie with the series. Confirm that the listing is the feature film rather than a trailer, recap or bonus entry.

Subtitles and English audio may be available on different dates or from different services. Check the player before you start a watch party so everyone has the same episode and version. This order is independent of provider: once you know which title corresponds to the movie and each season, follow the sequence above.
Quick answers

Should I watch JJK 0 before Season 1? You can, because it is a prequel, but Season 1 first is the recommended path for most newcomers. Where does it go? Between Season 1 and Season 2. What comes after Season 2? Season 3's Culling Game story. Is Season 3's first part complete? The official schedule says episode 59, Season 3 episode 12, aired March 26, 2026; check current US services for the dub and latest regional release.

Simple route: Season 1 → JJK 0 → Season 2 → Season 3. Use chronological order only if you deliberately want the events arranged by fictional timeline. For a first viewing, the original release sequence builds the world cleanly and gives the prequel room to feel like a meaningful expansion.

title: Fate Watch Order for Beginners: Release Order, Story Timeline and Best Starting Point
description: Fate has branching routes, a prequel and separate spin-offs. Start with a spoiler-aware recommendation, then compare anime release order with the visual novel's story structure.
keywords: Fate watch order for beginners, Fate Zero or Unlimited Blade Works first, Fate series timeline, Heaven's Feel order
summary: Fate is not one linear television series. Fate/stay night began as a visual novel with three routes—Fate, Unlimited Blade Works and Heaven's Feel—while Fate/Zero is a prequel and other titles branch into separate settings. For an anime-first newcomer, a clear spoiler-aware route is Unlimited Blade Works (TV) → the three Heaven's Feel films → Fate/Zero. This is a recommendation, not an official mandated order; release order and the source game's route order are different.
sourceLabel: TYPE-MOON official Fate/stay night route overview and anime catalog

references.label: TYPE-MOON: Fate/stay night routes and story introduction
TYPE-MOON: official anime catalog listing UBW, Heaven's Feel and Fate/Zero
TYPE-MOON: Unlimited Blade Works route overview
TYPE-MOON: Heaven's Feel route overview

sections: Start here: a spoiler-aware anime route

For an anime-first viewer who wants a direct, polished entry into the central Fate/stay night story, try Fate/stay night: Unlimited Blade Works (the television series, beginning with its prologue) → the three Heaven's Feel films → Fate/Zero. This sequence introduces the main conflict before returning to its earlier history, and it avoids using the prequel as a reader's very first explanation of the franchise.

This route is a practical recommendation, not an official rule. There is no one order that every Fate fan or creator says is mandatory. The original visual novel has three routes that unfold in a set order; anime adaptations were released at different times and do not reproduce that structure in one perfectly continuous television series.
The three routes explained simply

Fate/stay night begins with a young mage drawn into the Fifth Holy Grail War. The visual novel tells the conflict through three character-centered routes: Fate, Unlimited Blade Works and Heaven's Feel. TYPE-MOON's official overview identifies them separately, with Saber, Rin Tohsaka and Sakura Matou at their respective centers.

Each route is a different view of shared events, not three sequential seasons in which the same plot simply continues. They reveal different information and emphasize different relationships. That is why a route's adaptation can make another one feel less mysterious if watched first. Even if you never play the original game, knowing that the story branches explains why the anime lineup looks more complicated than a normal show list.
An easy route map
ANIME-FIRST, SPOILER-AWARE → Unlimited Blade Works TV → Heaven's Feel I, II, III → Fate/Zero.

RELEASE-HISTORY ROUTE → Fate/stay night (2006) → Fate/Zero → Unlimited Blade Works TV → Heaven's Feel trilogy. This follows major anime release order, but the 2006 adaptation blends and alters route material, so it is not a clean screen version of the visual novel's first route.

SOURCE-GAME ROUTE → Fate route → Unlimited Blade Works route → Heaven's Feel route. Choose the original visual novel if you want the source's intended branching structure and fuller internal narration.
Where Fate/Zero belongs

Fate/Zero is a prequel to Fate/stay night and depicts the earlier Holy Grail War. Watching it first follows the in-universe timeline, but it was released as a prequel for an audience that could already anticipate the later conflict. Some of its reveals and dramatic framing land differently if you already know the stay night setup.

If you love chronological storytelling and do not mind learning background before meeting the stay night leads, Zero first can work. If you are new and want the main characters and conflict introduced before the past is unpacked, watch it after UBW and Heaven's Feel. That is why the recommended route above places story chronology second to a gradual introduction.
Which UBW listing should you choose?

Look for the television series Fate/stay night: Unlimited Blade Works, not the standalone 2010 movie of the same route. The TV production has a prologue episode and a longer two-part story. A provider may label its halves as seasons or split cour listings; begin at the prologue and follow its episode order.

An official title can appear under multiple names—Fate/stay night [UBW], Fate/stay night: Unlimited Blade Works, or a platform's localized punctuation. Confirm that the synopsis refers to the TV series and check its episode count. A movie listing around 90 minutes is the earlier theatrical adaptation, not the full television version.
How to approach the 2006 Fate/stay night anime

The 2006 television adaptation is historically important and introduces the Fate/stay night world, but it was produced before the later UBW series and Heaven's Feel films. It mixes route elements and has a different adaptation style. If you are curious about the anime's history, watch it as an alternate entry after learning what the three routes mean.

If you decide to start with it, do not assume every plot point will be repeated exactly in UBW or the films. Each production has a different focus, and a character's role may change with the route being adapted. This is another reason an anime-only viewer can prefer a clearly labeled order rather than a single “chronological Fate timeline” that merges incompatible branches.
What counts as a spin-off?

Fate/Apocrypha, Fate/Grand Order, Fate/EXTRA Last Encore, Lord El-Melloi II's Case Files and Prisma Illya are among the other anime listed by TYPE-MOON. Their existence is one reason a complete franchise checklist can look endless. They do not all form chapters between the central stay night entries.

After you have watched one central stay night route and understand the Holy Grail War premise, pick spin-offs by genre or character interest. Some share concepts, organizations or familiar names; that does not automatically make them sequential seasons. A beginner does not need to watch every Fate-branded production to understand the central story.
A route through the source material

If you want the fullest version of Fate/stay night, the visual novel is the original source. It is interactive prose with three routes, so it can spend time inside a character's thoughts and choices in a way a film or television series cannot. The anime is a valid introduction, but it compresses material and makes route choices for the viewer.

TYPE-MOON's current product pages describe the three routes and identify the remastered game. Check the platform and edition available in your region before purchasing, because remaster availability and language support can differ. You can enjoy the anime without playing the game; the novel is an optional deeper version, not required homework.
Common mistakes to avoid

Do not start three unrelated spin-offs in a row because a watch-order graphic labels them “Fate 1, 2 and 3.” Do not watch the 2010 UBW movie when you meant the television series. Do not interpret the word prequel as proof that Fate/Zero must be first. And do not expect the Heaven's Feel films to retell the entire Fate/stay night story; they adapt a particular route.

If spoilers matter to you, avoid searching for “true ending,” “route order” or character fate before viewing. A beginner guide can answer where a title belongs without revealing its central reveals. The best watch order is the one that helps you enter the story with the intended amount of context and without making the branch structure feel like a puzzle you must solve.
Final recommendation

Start with UBW's TV version, continue to the three Heaven's Feel movies, then watch Fate/Zero. Choose the 2006 Fate/stay night series first only if you want release history or are comfortable with an older adaptation that blends routes. Play/read the visual novel if you want the original route order: Fate → UBW → Heaven's Feel.

Once the core is clear, explore spin-offs by interest instead of forcing them into one timeline. Fate is easier to enjoy when you see it as a group of related stories and adaptations, not a single forty-hour sequence with one officially correct playlist.

summary: The main anime path is Naruto (220 episodes) → Naruto: Shippuden (500 episodes) → The Last: Naruto the Movie → Boruto: Naruto Next Generations. For a spoiler-safe story placement, watch The Last after Shippuden episode 493 and before episodes 494–500. Most other Naruto movies are optional side stories. Boruto's television series later adapts the Boruto: Naruto the Movie story, so new viewers can start Boruto episode 1 instead of watching both versions back to back.

sections: The simple full-series route

NARUTO (original series, episodes 1–220) → NARUTO: SHIPPUDEN (episodes 1–493) → THE LAST: NARUTO THE MOVIE → SHIPPUDEN episodes 494–500 → BORUTO: NARUTO NEXT GENERATIONS. The placement of the film reflects its story position in the period after the war and before the final wedding-focused episodes.

Service catalogs may label Shippuden as seasons, collections or numbered episodes; VIZ lists it as a 500-episode series. Use the individual episode number on a trustworthy guide when your provider resets numbering each season. For the first Naruto series, episode 220 is the bridge into Shippuden, so do not stop at episode 219 if you want the complete TV transition.
Where The Last fits

The Last: Naruto the Movie is the key theatrical film to include for a main-story viewing. It takes place after the major war and before the epilogue stretch that leads to Naruto's adult life. A widely used spoiler-aware placement is after Shippuden episode 493 and before episodes 494–500, whose stories move toward the wedding.

Do not confuse its position with the order in which a streaming service lists specials. The movie may appear in a separate film carousel or under a franchise page. If you have already finished all 500 Shippuden episodes, you can still watch it; it simply works best before the final epilogue episodes.

If you prefer not to interrupt a completed binge, watching The Last after Shippuden episode 500 is also understandable: you will still follow the story, although the movie's events sit earlier than the wedding-centered epilogue. The episode-493 placement is a sequence recommendation, not a barrier that makes the film incomprehensible later. Use a spoiler-aware guide if you have skipped long anime-original blocks, because a suggested number can change when your route omits episodes.
Which Naruto movies can you skip?

Most of the Naruto and Shippuden theatrical films are self-contained adventures or alternate story material, so they are optional if your goal is the central TV plot. Watching them can be fun for more team missions and action, but a first-time viewer does not need to pause every few episodes to insert a film.

The Last is the important exception in a main-story guide because it bridges the main narrative to the characters' adult future. Boruto: Naruto the Movie is another special case: the Boruto television anime retells and expands its central story later. You can watch the movie for a concise version or follow the longer TV adaptation, but watching both in immediate sequence repeats a large portion of the same plot.
Filler: a useful route without false precision

The original Naruto has a long anime-original stretch late in its run. Many manga-focused guides mark episodes 136–219 as filler or anime-original, while episode 220 returns to an important transition. If you want a shorter manga-focused route, use a current episode guide for this stretch and make sure to watch the final transition episode rather than jumping blindly from 135 to Shippuden.

Shippuden mixes manga-adapted story with anime-original arcs and some mixed episodes. The official Naruto site labels several blocks as “ANIME ORIGINAL”; for example, its index identifies the Kakashi: Shadow of the Anbu Black Ops arc as original material and marks other story sections accordingly. That official label tells you the production status; it does not decide whether the arc is worth your time.
A practical filler decision tree
WANT THE MAIN MANGA STORY? → use an episode guide that separates manga-canon, mixed and anime-original episodes; skip only clearly standalone arcs, and check the first and last episode of a block.
CURIOUS ABOUT SIDE STORIES? → keep anime-original arcs that focus on a favorite character or offer extra time with the world. There is no penalty for watching them later.

UNSURE ABOUT A NUMBER? → read the official episode synopsis and compare multiple guides. Episode classifications sometimes vary because an installment can adapt a small manga scene and add a longer anime-only story around it.
Naruto → Shippuden → Boruto: what changes?

Naruto follows the lead character as a young ninja trying to earn acceptance and become Hokage. Shippuden resumes after a time skip, with a more experienced team and larger political conflict. The stories are connected, so starting with Shippuden sacrifices the early formation of Naruto's bonds with Sakura, Sasuke and Kakashi.

Boruto follows a later generation and can be watched after Shippuden. It is a separate ongoing sequel series with its own character focus. The official Naruto site announced episode 293 as the end of Boruto's Part One in March 2023; as of this guide's November 20, 2026 check, any continuation status or new release date should be confirmed against a new official announcement rather than inferred from an old hiatus notice.
How to watch Boruto without double coverage

If you are continuing directly from Shippuden, begin Boruto: Naruto Next Generations episode 1. The anime retells and expands the events associated with Boruto: Naruto the Movie in a later run of episodes, commonly identified as episodes 53–66. Viewers can either watch the movie first for the compact theatrical version or let the series reach its adaptation.

That choice is about pacing, not whether you understand the franchise. If you watch both, expect repeated events with differences and added scenes. A first-time viewer who prefers weekly television can skip the film and continue the series; someone who wants a film-length introduction to the next generation can watch the movie, then jump ahead to the next unadapted TV story using a reliable episode guide.
A film-inclusive release order for completionists

For fans who want every theatrical entry, use the release year and official title to build a separate movie watchlist, then insert optional films between arcs only when a distributor or production source gives a clear placement. Treat them as side stories when no precise placement is established. The exact gap between episodes is less important than avoiding a film spoiler for an arc you have not reached.

Do not copy a franchise timeline that combines manga events, novels, films and anime-original material into one rigid schedule without checking what it calls canon. Naruto's long animation history gives different lists different goals: release history, manga-only chronology or a casual fan marathon. State which goal you are following, and the list becomes much easier to trust.
Quick route recap

MAIN STORY: Naruto 1–220 → Shippuden 1–493 → The Last → Shippuden 494–500 → Boruto 1 onward. SHORTER MANGA-FOCUSED ROUTE: use an episode guide to skip clearly anime-original blocks, especially the late original-series stretch, but keep transition and mixed episodes.

Movies are bonuses except The Last for the cleanest main-story bridge. Boruto: Naruto the Movie is repeated and expanded by the television anime. If a platform's episode counts or season numbers differ, compare episode titles and use the official franchise index before skipping.

For most new viewers, 2011 is the easiest first watch: it adapts more of the manga, including the Chimera Ant arc, and has a clear endpoint. The 1999 version is a worthwhile alternate interpretation with a slower, moodier early stretch, but it does not cover the later arcs.

sections: The quick recommendation

Start with Hunter x Hunter (2011) if this is your first time. It is a fresh adaptation with 148 episodes, begins the main journey from the start, and continues through the Chimera Ant and Chairman Election arcs. It offers the most complete animated path for a new viewer, while still stopping before the manga's later Dark Continent material.

Choose the 1999 version if you want an alternate take on the early story, a slower build, and a moodier late-1990s production style. Nippon Animation lists 62 episodes for the original TV series. Several OVAs continue the story beyond that television run; treat them as the follow-on releases for that adaptation rather than as a second season of the 2011 series.
At a glance: two adaptations

HUNTER X HUNTER (1999) → 62-episode TV adaptation, followed by OVAs that continue into Yorknew and Greed Island material. Best for: atmosphere, slower early character work and historical comparison. Coverage: stops far earlier than the 2011 series.

HUNTER X HUNTER (2011) → 148-episode adaptation from the beginning through the Chairman Election. Best for: a cleaner all-in-one first watch and access to the Chimera Ant arc. Coverage: continues substantially further but does not adapt the entire ongoing manga.
These are not sequential seasons. The 2011 show restarts the story; do not finish episode 62 of the 1999 series and then begin episode 63 of the newer production.
How their openings differ

The 1999 production starts with a more gradual introduction and has time to linger on the mood of the Hunter Exam and the people Gon meets. Its older visual texture and quieter pacing can make the world feel more mysterious. That can be a strength if you enjoy patient setup, but it may feel dated to a viewer accustomed to faster modern edits.

The 2011 anime opens with a brighter color palette and a brisker adaptation rhythm. It presents the core premise quickly and uses contemporary animation conventions. Its first episode also establishes a key relationship with Kite earlier than the 1999 series does, closer to the manga's opening emphasis. That change is a point of comparison, not evidence that one version is universally correct.
Coverage: why 2011 reaches more story

The 1999 TV run ends during material that the later OVA releases continue. The OVA sequence moves beyond the television endpoint and carries the earlier adaptation through Yorknew City and the Greed Island storyline. This makes the 1999 route longer than its 62 TV episodes if you want to follow its continuation, but it still does not cover the later Chimera Ant and Chairman Election arcs.

Nippon TV's official page lists 148 episodes for the 2011 adaptation, and its episode 148 entry closes on Gon meeting his father. The adaptation covers Hunter Exam, Yorknew, Greed Island, Chimera Ant and Chairman Election. It does not adapt the manga's subsequent Dark Continent Expedition storyline, so 148 episodes means a substantial stopping point, not the end of the source story.
Tone and presentation

Fans often describe 1999 as darker and more atmospheric. That impression comes from direction, color, music, pacing and the way scenes are allowed to sit; the two adaptations do not turn the whole story into different genres. The later series has its own emotional intensity, especially as the scale of the conflict grows. Give each version a fair sample before deciding that one is childish or one is too dark.

Both series follow Gon, Killua, Kurapika and Leorio, but not every beat is staged or timed the same way. A remake comparison is most interesting when it focuses on adaptation choices: what gets emphasized, which scene is expanded, and how a change shapes audience expectations. A list of differences without the surrounding arc can make small edits sound like major continuity errors.
If you want to watch both

Watch 1999 TV → 1999 OVA continuations in their release order if you want the full older adaptation. Then watch the 2011 series from episode 1 as a separate retelling. You can reverse those two routes if you prefer to experience the modern version first and then compare its opening and early arcs with the older show.

Do not splice OVAs into the 2011 episode list. Their numbering and continuity belong to the 1999 production. Platform listings may place OVA episodes under a separate collection or omit them entirely, so confirm the exact title and release before assuming the old series is available as one continuous package.
Which version should you choose by viewing style?
I WANT THE MOST STORY IN ONE SERIES → 2011. Its 148 episodes carry the animated narrative through a major emotional checkpoint and into the Chairman Election.
I WANT A CLASSIC, SLOWER EARLY ADAPTATION → 1999, then its OVAs. Be comfortable with the fact that this route stops before the later arcs.

I WANT TO COMPARE DIRECTION → watch the 1999 Hunter Exam and early Yorknew material, then compare the same stories in 2011. Keep a notes list of pacing, color and character introductions rather than trying to declare a universal winner.
Where to go after episode 148

If the 2011 ending leaves you wanting more, the manga is the next source for story beyond the anime. Because the manga's release status can change, avoid relying on a fixed latest chapter number copied from an old guide. VIZ's official series page is a better place to check English chapters and current access terms on the day you plan to read.

The end of the anime is still an intentional emotional stopping point. It concludes a major stage of Gon's original goal, even though the wider world and manga story continue. You can pause there, read on, or return later; you do not need to switch to the 1999 OVAs expecting them to fill the missing post-2011 material.

The older route is useful for a comparison precisely because it is incomplete relative to the 2011 run. It gives Yorknew and Greed Island a different amount of time and ends before the later arcs. If you reach its television finale and want the old continuity to continue, search the exact OVA titles in order—Hunter x Hunter OVA, Greed Island, then Greed Island Final—rather than switching to the 2011 series mid-story.
Quick answers

Is the 1999 series a prequel to 2011? No, 2011 is a new adaptation from the start. Which version has more episodes? 2011 has 148 TV episodes; the 1999 broadcast itself has 62 before its OVA continuations. Which one covers Chimera Ant? The 2011 adaptation. Does either anime adapt the whole manga? No.

Best first watch: 2011. Best alternate: 1999 plus its OVAs. Best comparison: sample the same early arc in both. The official episode counts are useful facts; preferences about tone and pacing belong to each viewer.

title: Bleach Watch Order: Original Episodes, Thousand-Year Blood War and Filler

summary: The main Bleach order is the original 366-episode TV series followed by Bleach: Thousand-Year Blood War, whose concluding fourth part reached episode 50 in 2026. Films are optional for the central story. Viewers who want a manga-focused run can skip clearly anime-original blocks in the original series, including Bount, New Captain Shūsuke Amagai, Zanpakutō Unknown Tales and Gotei 13 Invading Army. Mixed episodes and arc boundaries need care; this guide explains how to skip without losing canon scenes.

sections: The clean story order

1. Bleach (the original television anime, episodes 1–366). 2. Bleach: Thousand-Year Blood War, Part 1: The Blood Warfare. 3. Part 2: The Separation. 4. Part 3: The Conflict. 5. Part 4: The Calamity, the concluding cour. As of November 2026, the official schedule lists TYBW episode 50 as the final scheduled distribution installment.

Some services label TYBW as Season 17 or use four separate seasonal entries. Others restart episode numbering at 1 within the new series. Search by the full subtitle and part name; do not assume that episode 367 is how a service labels its first TYBW episode. The original TV series and the new adaptation form one continuing story, but their catalogs are distinct.
At a glance: optional versus essential
ESSENTIAL MAIN PATH → original Bleach episodes 1–366 → all four Thousand-Year Blood War cours through episode 50.
OPTIONAL THEATRICAL FILMS → four animated feature films and other specials. They are not required to follow the core television plot; watch them as bonuses if you enjoy extra adventures.

MANGA-FOCUSED SHORTCUT → skip clearly anime-original blocks only after checking mixed-episode boundaries. The ranges below are common fan-guide classifications, not official episode tags supplied by the studio.
What the original series establishes

Bleach begins with Ichigo Kurosaki's ability to see spirits and his sudden responsibility as a Soul Reaper. The original anime introduces the human cast, Soul Society and later conflict in the order viewers first encountered them on television. That material is important setup for Thousand-Year Blood War, which expects you to understand the characters, powers and institutions already in play.

Do not begin with TYBW just because it is the current-looking series on a service homepage. It is the concluding manga arc, not a reboot or standalone Season 1. If you need to shorten the watch, use a carefully labeled filler guide inside the original run rather than jumping past the entire original series.
Major anime-original blocks to know

COMMONLY SKIPPED BLOCKS: Bount, episodes 64–108 in many episode guides; New Captain Shūsuke Amagai, episodes 168–189; Zanpakutō Unknown Tales and the following Beast Swords material, approximately episodes 228–266; Gotei 13 Invading Army, episodes 311–341. These long arcs were created for the television anime and are separate from the manga storyline.

Episode ranges can vary at their edges because some guides classify an episode as mixed or treat a transition episode separately. For example, Anime Filler List labels multiple Bleach episodes as mixed canon/filler. If you are doing a skip run, use its episode-by-episode list and retain any canon material the guide marks as mixed.

A safe skip routine is to pause at the start of a named filler block, confirm that the previous episode finishes the manga-based arc, and check the episode that resumes the main story. If the guide marks the boundary as mixed, keep that episode and skip only the clearly standalone stretch. This prevents a fan-made episode range from removing a character's first canon appearance.
Should you skip all filler?

Skip those blocks if your only goal is to follow the manga's central story as efficiently as possible. Keep them if you enjoy spending more time with the cast, want an anime-original conflict, or would like a pause before continuing the main arc. Some viewers enjoy the Zanpakutō story despite its non-manga origin; filler describes adaptation status, not quality.

Be aware that anime-original characters or references can appear in scenes around a filler arc. The manga story may not acknowledge them later, so a canon-only viewer can feel confused if they return after skipping an entire block and remember a side character. This is why a clear guide should name the arc and explain the skip, instead of just saying skip a random 40 episodes.
How Thousand-Year Blood War differs

Thousand-Year Blood War adapts the concluding manga arc after the original TV anime's long gap. It is presented in multiple cours and has a different production context from the 2004 series. Its official site describes it as the concluding arc, and the 2026 schedule notice specifically changed the broadcast dates for episodes 49 and 50 as the series approached its climax.

New scenes or expanded material in the TYBW anime should not be automatically treated like old filler. An adaptation can add, revise or stage material with the original creator's input; episode additions are not all equivalent. If you want to compare the anime to the manga, use the official episode and publication materials and identify what is confirmed versus what a fan guide infers.
Where the movies fit

The animated Bleach films are optional side stories for a first-time television watch. If you want to include them, place them during a gap in the original broadcast era according to their release and spoiler level, but there is no need to pause the main story for each movie. A film can be enjoyable even when its events are not needed to follow the manga-based ending.

Do not let a platform's playlist order dictate continuity. A streaming app may display a movie before the series because it is more recent or has a separate license. Watch the television series first if you are unsure. When a franchise has one clearly essential TV-to-TV progression and optional films, a simple core order is more useful than a wall of speculative chronology.
US platform and dub checks

The original series and TYBW may be licensed by different providers in the United States, and dubs can arrive on a different schedule from subtitles. Search the full subtitle and part number on your service. Check whether it lists the whole original run and whether the TYBW part is complete through episode 50 before planning a marathon.

Audio menus are title- and season-specific. If you want English audio or subtitles, open the player and verify the track for a particular episode rather than assuming every season has matching language options. Current availability is a moving catalog fact, so use the service listing and official on-air page when you publish a dated where-to-stream update.
Quick answers and recommended route

Do I have to watch the films? No. Is TYBW a sequel? It is a continuation and adaptation of the concluding arc; watch it after the original series. How many TYBW installments are listed as of November 2026? The official schedule reaches episode 50. Which fillers are easiest to identify? The long arcs named above, but use a mixed-episode guide at transition points.

Recommended route: Bleach episodes 1–366 → TYBW Parts 1–4 through episode 50. For a shorter version, skip only the anime-original blocks after checking episode edges. For a completionist route, watch the original TV series including filler, then continue into TYBW; add the films when you feel like an extra adventure.

title: Anime Sub vs Dub: What Changes, Which to Choose and When English Episodes Release
description: Subtitles and English dubs are two ways to enjoy anime, not a test of fandom. Compare translation, timing, accessibility and release schedules, then choose the version that fits you.
keywords: anime sub vs dub, subtitles or English dub, anime dub schedule, what is subbed and dubbed anime
summary: Subbed anime keeps Japanese audio with translated text; dubbed anime replaces the dialogue track with a localized performance, often with English captions available separately. Neither is automatically more authentic or better. A subtitle route can let you follow a weekly Japanese release sooner; a dub may make visual details easier to enjoy or support screen-free watching. Availability differs by title, season, episode and region, so the useful habit is checking the provider's language menu before you begin.
sourceLabel: Netflix and Crunchyroll official language availability guidance, checked November 20, 2026

references.label: Netflix Help: audio and subtitle options vary by title, location, profile and season
Crunchyroll Help: check audio and subtitles on each show page; language availability may vary by season
Netflix Help: change audio and subtitle language

sections: Sub and dub, in plain English

“A sub” usually means Japanese audio with subtitles in your chosen language. “A dub” means the dialogue is performed in another language—often English for a US release—while the music and sound effects remain part of the original mix or are adjusted as the production requires. Some releases also provide closed captions for the dub and subtitles designed for the Japanese track; those text tracks are not always identical.

People use subbed and dubbed as if each show has one permanent version, but a service can offer several audio tracks, subtitle styles and regional edits. A listing can have Japanese audio with English subtitles, English audio with English captions, or a different language combination. Always check the player for the exact season and episode you plan to watch.
Quick choice: which version should you try?
CHOOSE SUBTITLES IF → you like hearing the original Japanese performance, want to watch close to the Japanese release, or can comfortably read while following fast scenes.
CHOOSE AN ENGLISH DUB IF → reading subtitles distracts you, you want to look closely at animation, you watch while doing chores, or you prefer English voice performances.
TRY BOTH IF → a character's delivery, humor or emotional scene matters to you. Switch one episode or a few minutes; no one is grading your choice.
What actually changes between versions

A dub is a new vocal performance shaped by a translated script and recording direction. The English line may need to fit a character's mouth movement or match a line's emotional timing. That can make the wording shorter, more conversational or otherwise different from a subtitle. A subtitle is also a translation, not a word-for-word transcript of every Japanese syllable; translators make choices about tone, clarity and reading speed.

The performers bring their own interpretation, whether they speak Japanese or English. It is unfair to describe one language as inherently more expressive. A viewer may connect more strongly with a Japanese actor's breath and delivery, while another may love an English actor's timing. Performance, casting and adaptation vary by show; the format alone does not determine quality.
Subtitles: strengths and trade-offs

Subtitles preserve the original recorded dialogue and can be a good route for people who like hearing a performance in its original language. They may also be available sooner during a simulcast, because an English dub can require additional casting, recording, adaptation and quality review after the Japanese episode is ready.

The trade-off is attention. Fast conversations, unfamiliar names, signs and action can make reading harder, particularly on a small screen or if the subtitle timing is dense. Some platforms provide captions for sound and music; others offer dialogue-only subtitles or separate subtitle tracks. If you have a visual or reading accessibility need, test a scene before committing to a whole series.
English dubs: strengths and trade-offs

Dubs let a viewer keep their eyes on the image and can work well for younger viewers, people with reading differences, shared family watching or background listening. A strong dub can make jokes feel natural in English and help a viewer distinguish character voices quickly. It is also a creative performance, not a lesser shortcut.

The trade-off is timing and release cadence. A weekly English dub may begin after the subtitled broadcast and then release on its own schedule. A title may be dubbed only for selected seasons, or an older season may have a different cast or language menu. Never promise a dub date based on a general pattern; use the distributor's dated announcement for that exact show.
Why subtitles and dub scripts may not match

Subtitle lines are usually designed to be read quickly and fit the screen. Dub dialogue has to be spoken aloud and may be adjusted to the scene's rhythm and mouth movement. A translation can therefore be accurate in intent without matching word for word. Differences do not automatically mean one version is censored or dishonest; they can be ordinary localization choices.

Captions for an English dub may also differ from subtitles translated from Japanese, since they may follow the recorded English script. If you are studying translation or quoting dialogue, identify the audio and text track you are using. A line's exact wording can vary between a manga, subtitle, dub and edited broadcast.
How to check a real release schedule

Look at the streaming service's official announcement for the title, season and language. Confirm whether it says English dub premiere, names a weekly day or gives only a first episode date. A premiere date is not automatically the date for every episode; a weekly release can pause for production or holiday reasons.

On Netflix, the help center says the available languages depend on the title and can vary by location or season. Crunchyroll likewise recommends checking each title's details page and notes that language availability can differ between seasons and episodes. For a specific week, the platform's current page is stronger evidence than an old social media schedule.

Language catalogs can vary for practical reasons such as licensing, device support, downloads and region. Netflix's help page explains why a title or even a particular season may not show a track that appears elsewhere; Crunchyroll directs viewers to each show detail page and warns that options can differ by season or episode. That makes the in-player menu the right last check when someone asks whether a dub is available today.
A low-friction way to decide

Start an episode in your preferred default format, then ask three questions: Am I following the plot without strain? Am I enjoying the actors' performances? Am I missing visual details or feeling pulled away from the scene? If the answer is no to any of these, switch formats. You are allowed to watch some episodes dubbed and others subbed.

Consider your setting. A commute with noisy audio might favor subtitles and headphones; a workout or cooking session may favor a dub. A group with mixed preferences can turn on an available subtitle track while listening to the English dub. There is no universal proper viewing setup outside of a specific creator or release instruction.
Quick answers

Is sub always more authentic? It preserves the original-language performance, but the subtitles are still a localized translation. Is dub inferior? No; it is a distinct performance and adaptation. Are English episodes always a week late? No; schedules depend on the title and distributor. Can different seasons have different tracks? Yes, providers explicitly say language options can vary by season or episode.

Best advice: select the version that lets you enjoy the story and check the exact player options. If you care about early access, follow the subtitled schedule. If you care about looking at the animation or listening in English, check the dub status and its own release calendar. Then spend less time defending the choice and more time watching.

title: Anime Filler vs Canon: What You Can Skip Without Missing the Story
description: Learn the difference between manga-canon, anime-original, mixed and recap episodes, then use a careful skip method that protects important scenes.
keywords: anime filler vs canon, what anime filler means, can I skip anime filler, manga canon episode guide
summary: Canon usually means material adapted from the original manga or other designated source; filler is a fan term for anime-original story material that is not needed to follow that source plot. Real episodes can be mixed, recap, anime-canon or partially adapted, so a one-line skip list can be risky. This guide shows how to read episode classifications, use Naruto and Bleach as examples, and decide whether skipping helps your own watch.
sourceLabel: NARUTO OFFICIAL episode guide: examples of anime-original arc labels

references.label: NARUTO OFFICIAL: Shippuden index labels anime-original blocks
Anime Filler List: Naruto mixed, canon and filler classifications (secondary reference)
Anime Filler List: Bleach mixed, canon and filler classifications (secondary reference)
VIZ: official Shonen Jump manga catalog for checking source chapters

sections: The basic difference

Canon is a shorthand for story material recognized as part of a work's primary continuity. For a manga adaptation, viewers often mean scenes drawn from the original manga. Filler is a fan label for material the anime added, often to avoid catching up to a manga that was still being written. It can be a whole arc, a short detour, a recap, or extra scenes woven into a canon episode.

Those labels are practical, but they are not a universal legal or production taxonomy. A franchise may treat an anime-original sequel, movie or game story as part of its continuity, while a manga-only guide calls it non-manga canon. Before skipping something, ask canon according to which source? A useful guide states its method rather than presenting one fan classification as an official judgment.
Four episode labels worth separating

MANGA-CANON → adapts manga chapters or scenes central to the source story. ANIME-ORIGINAL → created for the screen version and not present in the manga chapters being adapted. MIXED → combines source events with newly added scenes or transitions. RECAP → repeats earlier footage or summarizes past events.

ANIME-CANON is sometimes used for original material that later episodes or official story planning treat as continuity. The term varies by fandom and series. A production's official site may label an arc anime original without saying that it is worthless or that viewers are forbidden to consider it part of a broader continuity.
Why filler exists

A weekly television adaptation may need to keep airing while the manga remains close to the anime's current point. A studio can create an original side story, extend a sequence, add character scenes, or schedule a recap to give the source material time to move forward. These are production choices with different effects on pacing and story continuity.

That history helps explain why one franchise can have distinct types of extra material. A 40-episode anime-original arc can usually be skipped as a block if you want only manga events. A 30-second added conversation in the middle of an adapted episode is harder to isolate and may matter emotionally even if it is not a manga panel. Skip filler is not a perfect button.
An episode can be mixed

Mixed episodes are the biggest trap in simple skip lists. A guide may classify an episode as partly filler because it contains original material, while another resource marks it canon because the important manga scene remains. If you skip the whole episode, you can lose an introduction, a reveal or the setup for the next manga-based installment.

Check the classification key before following a list. Some sites use mixed canon/filler as a separate category; some collapse mixed episodes into one of the other labels. If a skip range ends at episode 108 and episode 109 is marked mixed, confirm what content continues before jumping. The boundary matters more than an attractive graphic.
Examples: Naruto and Bleach

The official Naruto site labels particular Shippuden blocks anime original. It identifies episodes 442–462 as the Paradise Life on a Boat block and labels the Kakashi: Shadow of the Anbu Black Ops arc as original. That official production label is a helpful source, while fan guides can add scene-level manga comparisons and recommendations about which side stories they enjoy.

Bleach episode guides mark long anime-original blocks such as Bount, New Captain Shūsuke Amagai, Zanpakutō Unknown Tales and Gotei 13 Invading Army. Episode ranges at their edges can differ because some entries contain mixed material. This is why a block-level shortcut should link readers to an episode-level reference and say what classification system it uses.
How to make a safe skip plan

STEP 1: Choose your goal. A manga-only catch-up, a completionist watch and a character-focused rewatch need different lists. STEP 2: Use a guide that clearly defines canon, filler and mixed. STEP 3: Check official episode summaries for the first and last item in any long range.

STEP 4: Keep mixed episodes unless the guide explains exactly which source scenes they contain. STEP 5: If you are confused after a jump, go back to the previous episode synopsis before looking up plot summaries that may spoil you. This method takes a minute longer than blind skipping and can save an entire arc's worth of context.
Is anime-original material worth watching?

Often, yes—if you enjoy the characters and have time. A non-manga arc may give a side character a mission, try a different tone, or allow the original animation staff to explore the world. Some viewers dislike the pacing; others count certain filler episodes among their favorites. The label describes where the material came from, not whether it is good.

If your goal is to reach the current manga-adapted plot quickly, skipping long original blocks is reasonable. If your goal is to enjoy a long series at your own pace, watch the episodes and decide for yourself. A guide should make both options easy instead of shaming viewers for watching or skipping.
Movies, specials and later continuity

Do not assume that every non-manga movie is disposable or that every anime-original episode must be included. A movie can be a side adventure, an alternate version, a manga story arc or a bridge explicitly acknowledged by later continuity. Check the official synopsis and franchise notes before placing it in a canon list.

Likewise, an anime can diverge from its source and then continue its own storyline. In that situation, manga canon is one useful comparison but it is not the only continuity that matters. For Fullmetal Alchemist, for example, the 2003 anime becomes a separate adaptation rather than a short filler detour on the way to Brotherhood. Separate adaptations need separate episode guides.
Reliable sources and fan episode guides

Start with the publisher's manga catalog or the official anime episode page. These establish what the source series is and how the production labels its own arcs. For chapter-level comparisons, use a licensed chapter or volume rather than a fan transcript. A licensed source is especially valuable when a show uses different titles or numbering across regions.

Fan-maintained episode databases are useful for mapping a long episode list, but they are secondary references. Their definitions can differ and they sometimes disagree on mixed episodes or canon status. A trustworthy article should identify that classification as an editorial guide, link the source, date when it was checked, and avoid claiming the studio itself calls every disputed episode filler.
Quick answers

Can I skip filler? Usually you can skip clearly standalone anime-original arcs if you want the manga plot. Can mixed episodes be skipped? Not safely without checking which source scenes they contain. Is filler always bad? No. Does canon always mean better? No; it only describes relationship to a continuity or source.

Use the shortest answer that fits your viewing goal. For a first watch, keep episodes unless pacing is bothering you. For a manga-only route, skip clearly marked blocks and preserve mixed episodes. For a completionist route, watch everything and treat filler as optional world-building. A good guide helps you choose; it does not tell you what you are allowed to enjoy.

sections: Preview notice

Chapter 40 has not been released yet. This article is a preview based on the officially released Chapter 39, not a review of Chapter 40. An original Chapter 40 review will follow after the chapter’s official release.
Where Chapter 39 leaves the story

Chapter 39 turns Boruto and Sarada’s rescue into a team fight. Sarada uses Ohirume to pull Code into range, giving Boruto the opening to land Rasengan: Uzuhiko. Code is down, but the chapter does not treat that as a clean resolution: his artificial hand begins to glow as he tries to move.

Elsewhere, Jura learns that Boruto is at the hideout, while Kawaki’s conversation with Himawari makes their disagreement about Boruto more personal. Chapter 40 has several threads to pick up, but none has a confirmed outcome yet. Chapter 39 is available now through [MANGA Plus](https://mangaplus.shueisha.co.jp/viewer/1029603), and VIZ lists it as the latest chapter.
Code’s glowing hand is a question, not an answer

The glow is Chapter 39’s sharpest unanswered question. Code has taken Uzuhiko and is struggling to get up, yet the final image hints that something is still happening. Chapter 40 could show whether the hand is part of a countermeasure, a reaction to the attack, or simply a signal that Code is not finished.

For now, those are possibilities, not confirmed explanations. The story has left Code conscious and angry, but it has not shown that he can overcome Uzuhiko. The next chapter may clarify the glow—or leave it as a brief warning while Boruto and Sarada focus on getting away.

Code’s position also creates a useful test for Boruto. If Code can still move, Boruto has to decide whether to spend time restraining him or use the exit he marked. A short delay could matter if Jura is already on his way. The glowing hand may therefore matter less as a new power reveal than as the detail that keeps the escape uncertain.
Can Boruto and Sarada escape before Jura arrives?

Boruto has marked a route out of the hideout, but Code’s Claw Marks have made the area difficult to leave safely. Kashin Koji also cannot give the group a reliable countdown to Jura’s arrival. That leaves Boruto and Sarada balancing two priorities: dealing with Code and keeping an escape route open.

Chapter 40 may continue directly from the fight, showing whether Boruto’s pin still offers a safe exit and whether Sarada can keep helping after the effort she has already spent. Their coordinated attack gives them a moment of advantage, but the chapter has not established that they control the situation.

That distinction matters because a successful hit is not the same as a completed rescue. Boruto still needs to get Sarada out, and Koji’s plans may change if the group learns Jura has reached the hideout. The next chapter could turn a tactical win into a hurried retreat rather than immediately starting a second full fight.
What Jura believes about Boruto

Jura leaves the bookstore after Hidari reports Boruto’s location. Furuta tells him to kill Boruto, relying on the Leaf’s mistaken public story about him. Jura’s next encounter with Boruto could therefore begin with a dangerous misunderstanding.

A confrontation is possible, especially if Jura reaches the hideout before the group escapes. But Chapter 39 does not confirm that they will meet in Chapter 40. It also leaves open whether Jura will act on Furuta’s instructions exactly as given, or whether his own curiosity will affect what he does next.

That curiosity is one reason the bookstore scene may matter beyond its comic tone. Jura has been learning about the human world through books and conversation, yet he leaves with a simple order shaped by false information. If he meets Boruto, what Jura has observed for himself may begin to compete with what other people have told him.
Himawari and Kawaki still have a choice to face

The chapter’s home scene gives the larger conflict a personal edge. Himawari continues to believe in Boruto, while Kawaki says he will eliminate Boruto if Momoshiki takes control. He asks her to choose between the Leaf and her brother, but she does not give him a final answer.

Amado’s scientific ninja tool toad then asks Kawaki for help. Chapter 40 could return to that request and clarify what Amado needs from him. It may also show how Kawaki responds to Himawari’s belief in Boruto. Neither question has been answered yet, so the preview can only point to the tension the story has set up.

If the chapter returns to the Uzumaki home, the most meaningful development may be a small change in how Kawaki handles Himawari’s answer, rather than an immediate fight. His position is firm, but the scene puts him in front of someone who loves Boruto and still hopes their family can be restored. The story has made that conflict intimate before it makes it physical.
Konoha’s internal pressure is still building

Mitsuki is being questioned by Kobu until Shikamaru steps in. That brief scene keeps the village’s struggle moving alongside the action at Code’s hideout. Chapter 40 could return to the interrogation and show what Shikamaru is trying to protect—or it may hold that thread while the immediate danger around Boruto takes priority.

The chapter may also build on Koji’s admission that his future sight cannot account for every change. Sarada’s choice to confront Code went against his recommendation, and the outcome shows why the characters cannot rely on a single forecast to settle every decision.

Koji may have to revise his plan as events keep moving outside his predictions. Chapter 39 has already shown Sarada acting on what she saw from Hidari, not only on what Koji believes will happen. That does not make his guidance useless; it means Chapter 40 can keep the future uncertain even when the characters have good information.
What could Chapter 40 focus on

Chapter 40 could focus on the immediate consequences of Uzuhiko: what Code’s glowing hand indicates, whether Boruto and Sarada can escape, and whether Jura reaches them. It could also shift back to Kawaki, Himawari, Amado’s request, or the situation in Konoha.

Those threads do not all need equal space in the next chapter. A focused continuation of the hideout scene could answer the most urgent question first, then use a final scene to reconnect the fight with the wider village conflict. Or the story may delay the confrontation and spend more time on Kawaki’s decision. Both remain speculation until Chapter 40 is released.
Chapter 40 release date and where to read

As of November 20, 2026, VIZ’s official chapter listing shows Chapter 39, dated November 19, as the latest release; it does not list a Chapter 40 date. A release window should not be treated as confirmed until the publisher posts it.

Readers can catch up with Chapter 39 on [MANGA Plus](https://mangaplus.shueisha.co.jp/viewer/1029603) and follow [VIZ’s official series listing](https://www.viz.com/shonenjump/chapters/boruto-two-blue-vortex) for release information. The full Chapter 40 review will follow after the chapter is officially available.
